title: Showcase: the gadget demo
summary: Demo the badge, the dice or the breadboard circuit to the family, one real bug included and told proudly.

figure.alt: A showcase layout: the chosen gadget (badge, dice or breadboard circuit) with its battery on the bench, a phone positioned to record it, and the family watching from one side. Text below lists the demo order: say what it does, show it live, then tell one bug proudly.

items.s: 1 say what it does   2 show it live

steps.title: Run the demo
steps.body:
Pick one gadget to demo: the name badge, the shake-to-roll dice, or the breadboard circuit with its button.

Get ready:

1. Set your gadget up before anyone is watching.
2. Clip on the battery pack so it just works the moment you press play.

Run the demo:

1. Say what your gadget does, before you do it.
2. Show it live: scroll your name, shake for a random roll, or press the button and make the LED answer.
3. Pick the one bug that gave you the most trouble this sprint.
4. Say what you expected to happen.
5. Say what actually happened instead.
6. Say the exact step that showed you where the bug was hiding.

Tell the bug proudly, like a scientist reporting a real finding, not like an apology.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo of your gadget mid-demo, or a short video of the whole demo, bug and all.

extras.title: Add a second bug to the story
extras.body:
Most demos only tell one bug story. Add a second, different one.

1. Look back at your bug diary from weeks 1 to 3 and pick a second bug.
2. Write one sentence for what you expected to happen.
3. Write one sentence for what actually happened instead.
4. Write one sentence for the exact step that showed you where it was hiding.
5. Practice telling both bug stories back to back, in under one minute total.
6. Run the demo again for the family, with both bugs included.

What to notice: a demo with two real bugs sounds more like a scientist's report, not less put together.

extras.title: Give your gadget one new trick for the demo
extras.body:
What is one thing your gadget cannot do yet that would make the demo better?

Add exactly one new behaviour to the badge, the dice, or the breadboard circuit.

It must add exactly one new behaviour to a gadget you already built.
It must have one number you choose by testing, like a pause or a cutoff.
It must be shown to someone in your house before the real demo.

Sketch your idea on paper first.

How to know it works: someone in your house notices the new trick without you pointing it out.

extras.title: How much has the battery's push faded?
extras.body:
Find out whether the battery pack's voltage is the same running your badge as it is sitting unused.

1. Predict first: guess how many volts the multimeter will read across the battery pack's two wires while the badge is off. Write your number in the Maker's Log.
2. Set a multimeter to measure DC volts and touch the two probes to the battery pack's wires while the badge is off.
3. Turn the badge on and read the voltage again while it runs.
4. Write down both readings in the Maker's Log.

Compare: was your prediction close to the reading with the badge off, and did turning the badge on change the number?

Teach it: tell a grown-up in two sentences why a battery's push can drop a little the moment it starts doing work.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
